title: Review: Elysian Punkuccino
summary:

This surprisingly delightful blend of beer styles that is built around a complex mix of Stumptown cold brew coffee, cinnamon, nutmeg, lactose, various malts, German Northern Brewer hops, and three different additions of pumpkin to the…

The post Review: Elysian Punkuccino appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Take a seasonal pumpkin ale and mix it with a classic milk stout and what do you get? This surprisingly delightful blend of beer styles that is built around a complex mix of Stumptown cold brew coffee, cinnamon, nutmeg, lactose, various malts, German Northern Brewer hops, and three different additions of pumpkin to the kettle.

It’s a near-perfect mix of both coffee and pumpkin spice flavors, heavy on the nutmeg up front, giving the attack a distinct gingerbread quality. The coffee rolls in quickly from there, though it’s amply balanced by hops to keep it from taking over completely. As the malts join the party, the beer bounces among a trinity of elements — pumpkin cake, milky coffee, and the doughy essence of a lightly hopped lager. Any one of these on their own may not have impressed, but what Elysian has done in the combination is nothing short of genius. Probably my favorite autumn brew I’ve tasted to date.

6% abv.

A- / $7 per 22 oz bottle (cans typically available in mixed packs)

The premise remains rooted in Alpine traditions: Teroldego and Marzemino are harvested off hillside vineyards in the…

The post Review: 2025 Mezzacorona Dinotte Red Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Mezzacorona’s Ventessa lineup already made its case for Trentino as a place worth considering when looking for a proper budget wine buy, so Dinotte was presumably christened for mood rather than any darkness in the glass or otherwise.

The premise remains rooted in Alpine traditions: Teroldego and Marzemino are harvested off hillside vineyards in the granite-heavy Dolomites, with the altitude performing labor usually attributed to the winemaker rather than the mountain. Then, for a bit of complexity, a bit of Merlot is thrown into the mix. Cool nights at that elevation produce brightness in the bottle, one of those  claims in the wine trade that sounds like a sales pitch until the glass proves it isn’t. What shows up are aromas of blackberry and red currant, tempered by French oak. There’s a savory streak running through the palate, with pencil lead and granite supporting the darker fruit. Touches of anise, clove and nutmeg cut through on the finish as the fruit recedes. It pairs quite well with a quality piece of dark chocolate or a small charcuterie board, but can also stand firmly on its own.

B / $11

The post Review: Whiskey Jypsi Gibson Tonewood: The Collective appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Here’s a new collaboration for you: Whiskey Jypsi partnered with Gibson — the guitar makers — to “reverse the familiar relationship between guitars and whiskey. Guitar makers have used whiskey barrel wood for years. With Tonewood, Whiskey Jypsi and Gibson flipped the idea: toasted maple tonewood offcuts from Gibson’s broader guitar-building process, wood already prized for resonance and character, are reimagined for whiskey finishing.” The release coincides with the launch of a new Eric Church guitar called The Epiphone, though its details are beyond the scope of Drinkhacker’s coverage, I fear.

There are two Tonewood whiskeys coming out. The first is a very limited offering (250 bottles) called Tonewood: Vol. 1, made from 20 and 14 year old whiskey stocks finished with toasted Gibson maple offcuts. The second is a more available spirit called Tonewood: The Collective, reviewed here, which uses younger whiskey stocks — 36% 14-year-old American whiskey from a bourbon mashbill (84% corn / 8% rye / 8% malted barley) and 64% 8-year-old straight bourbon (75% corn / 21% rye / 4% malted barley) — as its base. It’s finished on those same Gibson maple offcuts.

Whiskey Jypsi Gibson Tonewood: The Collective Review

The nose here is clean and quite sweet, the maple influence obvious from the get-go. Gently infused with gingery baking spices, a syrupy aroma emerges in short order, evoking Sunday pancakes with a side of chocolate milk. Oak is toasty and soothing, well-integrated into a pleasant and rounded whole. Indeed, it smells exactly what you imagine a freshly constructed acoustic guitar might smell like.

The palate continues the theme, and is perhaps even sweeter than the nose suggests, the maple quickly ceding way to notes of milk chocolate, then some mint. Caramel and toffee build from there, though eventually they give way to a more bready, toasty quality that grips the finish. Combined with the lingering spice notes and the not insignificant sweetness, the whiskey ultimately gives the impression of cinnamon rolls, though a touch of cayenne adds just the lightest sense of heat to the fade-out.

Solid, to be sure, but it’s firmly sweet tooth material.

103 proof.

A- / $199

The post Review: NV Nicolas Feuillatte Brut and Rose Champagne (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve written about the Champagnes of Nicolas Feuillatte several times, but here’s a fresh look at two of the operation’s most available bottlings from the “Reserve Exclusive” series — a nonvintage brut and a rose, both seen here in their 2020 incarnations. Both are available in standard bottles and in 187ml “splits” that can be consumed with nothing more than a straw.

Update 2026: We’re looking at these iconic bottles through a fresh lens, six years later.

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Champagne (2020) – There’s lots of toasty brioche up top, then a lively fruit component comes into focus. Apples and pears, plus a tropical spin, give this Brut lots of crispness and life, but the orchard notes fade away in fairly short order, leaving behind a reprise of toasted bread and a hint of Christmas spice. A- / $39 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Champagne (2026) – The Champagne’s house style is very much intact. The nose shows apple, pear, lemon drop, and lightly buttered brioche. The palate follows the nose with well-integrated notes of apple, pear, and toast. It is slightly sweet but that comes from the fruit, and it is certainly not cloying. As Chris noted tasting an earlier bottle, the finish is a bit short. But the bubbles are small and plentiful, providing a lovely, silky mouthfeel and there is medium to high acidity, promising this will pair with food nicely. -RL A- / $39 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Rose Champagne (2020) – Less overwhelmingly fruity than you might expect, with notes of carnations, roses, and marshmallow fluff dominating. At the same time, it’s not particularly sweet, though a cherry and strawberry character on the back end work well with the creamy character up top. Less “serious” than the Brut, but certainly summery and festive. A- / $56 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

NV Nicolas Feuillatte Reserve Exclusive Brut Rosé Champagne (2026) – A nose showing enjoyable aromas of lemon icing on buttery shortbread. The mousse is aggressive, offering a torrent of small bubbles, maybe too much. With a little time in the glass, they start to settle down, but fans may find the effusive effervescence a plus. The palate follows the nose, with bright lemon citrus coming first and yeasty brioche following. The wine shows medium acidity, and it will both pair nicely with food and be enjoyable on its own. -RL A- / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE]

title: Review: Non-Alcoholic Wines from French Bloom
summary:

It’s a perpetual trust-fall exercise, hoping whoever is on the other side bottling the stuff actually cares that it tastes like something in the same postal code as the alcohol-filled alternative. Enter French Bloom, a venture co-founded by ex-Michelin guide director Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger and…

The post Review: Non-Alcoholic Wines from French Bloom appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Non-alcoholic wine can still feel like an immense leap of faith. It’s a perpetual trust-fall exercise, hoping whoever is on the other side bottling the stuff actually cares that it tastes like something in the same postal code as the alcohol-filled alternative. Enter French Bloom, a venture co-founded by ex-Michelin guide director Maggie Frerejean-Taittinger and model Constance Jablonski, arriving with a pair of options timed almost with precision to the entire grueling holiday gauntlet, and the inevitable cleansing of Dry January. They are also the official non-alcoholic sparkling wine of Formula 1, a sport whose relationship to sobriety seems complicated by the customary champagne showers in the winner’s circle.

NV French Bloom Le Rosé – Filled with rose petal and red berry character, followed by notes of guava and white peach on the palate. There’s a curious blend of white tea and rhubarb lingering on the finish, providing a tart pinch as it fades. The mouthfeel is about as close to bubbly as it can get, though. A nice Sunday brunch accompaniment, especially when served with a sliced strawberry as garnish. B+ / $44

NV French Bloom Le Blanc – There’s some complexity working here: nuts, Granny Smith apple, a little honey, and an oxidative thing happening, reading as intentional rather than a bottle gone rogue. The palate leans into apple crumble territory, but the middle sags the way anything missing non-alcoholic tends to sag, as a tent with one pole pulled. It finishes quite tart with a touch of lemon zest, propped up entirely by acid doing the heavy lifting alcohol usually handles. B+ / $39

title: Review: Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels
summary:
Angel’s Envy has built its reputation on the idea that a whiskey’s journey need not end with its initial maturation. Since the introduction of its port finished bourbon, the Louisville-based whiskey maker has explored the effects of secondary maturation, from the Caribbean rum casks used for its rye whiskey, first released in 2013, to the…

The post Review: Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Angel’s Envy has built its reputation on the idea that a whiskey’s journey need not end with its initial maturation. Since the introduction of its port finished bourbon, the Louisville-based whiskey maker has explored the effects of secondary maturation, from the Caribbean rum casks used for its rye whiskey, first released in 2013, to the more unusual cask combinations featured in its limited releases.

For Volume 6 of the Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection, Master Distiller Owen Martin pulls out all the stops, bringing together peach brandy casks, toasted American oak, and toasted French oak. The foundation is rye whiskey made from a mashbill of 95% rye and 5% malted barley. Unlike Angel’s Envy’s standard rye, which was distilled in Indiana, this release draws on whiskey from two undisclosed Kentucky distilleries. The result is a meeting of grain, fruit, and wood, with three different finishing regimens shaping the final blend.

The whiskey was initially barreled between June 2014 and March 2018. Before secondary maturation, the youngest component spent 6 years, 6 months, and 6 days in oak, while the oldest aged for 11 years, 5 months, and 24 days. Following their respective finishes, the whiskeys were blended, bringing the total time spent in oak to between 8 and 11 years.

The younger component was finished primarily in toasted oak casks. The older component spent most of its finishing period in peach brandy casks, though some of it also went into toasted oak. In the final blend, 54.5% consists of whiskey aged for at least eight years, while the remaining 45.5% comprises whiskey aged between 10 and 11 years.

Peach brandy-finished whiskey accounts for 37.7% of the blend. Another 35.4% was finished in first- and second-fill toasted French oak casks, while the remaining 26.9% spent its finishing period in toasted American oak.

The peach brandy casks are 53 gallon ex-bourbon barrels that previously held peach brandy for at least three years. The brandy was distilled from a variety of clingstone peaches, primarily Dixon and Halford, along with freestone varieties, mainly Elberta and Big Red. The rye whiskey spent 15 to 23 months in these casks, entering at 114.5 proof.

Meanwhile, the toasted French and American oak finishes lasted between six and 12 months in custom heavy-toast barrels supplied by Kelvin Cooperage and Independent Stave Company. The whiskey entered these casks at 112.4 proof. After blending, the whiskey reached a natural harvest proof of 110.

With nearly a decade or more in oak for much of the blend, three finishing regimens, and peach brandy made from several varieties of peaches, Angel’s Envy has assembled an unusual take on Kentucky rye whiskey. How does this union of rye, peach brandy, and toasted oak turn out? Is it a little slice of Heaven in a glass? Let’s find out!

Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection Rye Finished in Peach Brandy and Toasted Oak Barrels Review

The nose opens with mildly sweet tea and honey. The sweetness is present, though likely not enough to satisfy many Southerners. Peach brandy makes its presence known without pushing the whiskey into overly sweet territory. Nutmeg joins the bouquet, accompanied by a floral note of orange blossom. As the whiskey sits in the glass, dusty oak arrives late, adding another dimension to the nose. I appreciate how clearly the peach brandy casks make their mark without dominating the whiskey.

On the palate, the peach brandy influence is immediate, though the fruit is less juicy, skewing a bit earthy, bringing to mind dehydrated peaches. A mild cinnamon note follows, with a natural spice quality rather than the artificial flavor of cinnamon gum. The mid-palate introduces cantaloupe, joined by ginger spice, with a pleasantly dry mouthfeel.

The finish brings more oak to the forefront, along with a brief sensation of chewing on a No. 2 pencil. That quickly gives way to cantaloupe rind and white pepper before circling back to the earthy, dried peach note found earlier in the tasting.

I consider this release a major success. Finishing whiskey in multiple cask types can easily result in one influence overpowering the others, but Owen Martin has brought together peach brandy, toasted French oak, and toasted American oak to excellent effect. Each finishing regimen makes its presence known without overwhelming the others. The result is an unusual, high-quality rye whiskey that, in my estimation, justifies its price.

106.4 proof.

A / $200 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

summary:

And so by 1996, he was digging hundreds of soil pits, studying the climate patterns and learning what his land could do. The winery was established four years…

The post Review: 2021 Brassfield Estate Cabernet Sauvignon High Valley AVA appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 1973, Jerry Brassfield bought a sprawling cattle ranch in Clearlake Oaks, designed to be a retreat from hectic city life. Then the neighbors began planting grapes. And so by 1996, he was digging hundreds of soil pits, studying the climate patterns and learning what his land could do. The winery was established four years later, the first vines went in the following year, and the inaugural vintage, made from leased fruit, soon followed. Estate wines arrived in 2005 from vines planted beside an old volcano. That same year, High Valley won its own appellation, a rare east-to-west valley where cool ocean air lingers through the night. Today, Brassfield has 500 acres planted across nearly 5,000, leaving the rest of the land to the wildlife. And now, we are uncorking its flagship wine for the first time.

Aromas of cassis and overripe plum rise from the glass first, undercut by tones of black licorice and damp earth. On the palate, blueberry provides a lingering youthful character at first, eventually receding to a vibrant combination of blackberry, orange peel and rosemary. Dark chocolate wraps around the fruit on the lingering finish, while hints of black truffle and minerality add depth. There’s quite a bit going on here, and it somehow holds together nicely. Wines with this much layering and polish usually come affixed with a price tag demanding some sort of occasion. This one doesn’t. It is remarkably fair in cost, and is the sort of bottle you can open on a humdrum weeknight and still feel you’ve been treated to something special.

A- / $35

title: Review: Elijah Craig Small Batch PGA Championship Edition (Updated 2026)
summary:

In 2024 the brand launched its second golf-inspired limited release as a follow-up to its recent Ryder Cup edition. By 2026, Elijah Craig PGA Edition had expanded to a second edition.…

The post Review: Elijah Craig Small Batch PGA Championship Edition (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Elijah Craig sure loves golf — or rather, getting people to drink while they’re playing or watching golf. Anything to liven things up, amirite?

In 2024 the brand launched its second golf-inspired limited release as a follow-up to its recent Ryder Cup edition. By 2026, Elijah Craig PGA Edition had expanded to a second edition. And here’s the shocker: It turns out these are not just novelty whiskeys to give your dad for Christmas, they’re well-designed spirits that are, shockingly, available for a song.

We presume more are coming, and we’ll cover each one in turn here.

Elijah Craig Small Batch 2024 PGA Championship Edition Review

Now this is what I call a gimmick: This limited release was made with barrels from rickhouse P (25%), 1G (61%) and A (14%). P-G-A. Get it? You got it! That’s the catch, so let’s see where it takes us. Slightly grassy on the nose — intentional? — with a stronger spice bill than usual, predominantly featuring cloves and powdered ginger. Soothing brown sugar notes open up with some airtime, but it takes a while to get there.

The palate is warming but not hot, offering an immediate slug of bright cherry fruit, backed up by plenty of wood. Black pepper come into focus in time, giving the brown sugar notes at the core of the spirit some oomph. More toasty oak on the finish, followed finally by a spoonful of crunchy peanut butter and a touch more clove. Well-rounded but not overwhelmingly complex, this is a fine, versatile bourbon at a surprisingly affordable price — gimmick or no. 94 proof. A- / $37 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Elijah Craig Small Batch 2026 PGA Championship Edition Review

A much different whiskey, with a far higher proof and drawn from different rickhouses: Heaven Hill Distillery’s N and S rickhouses, honoring the Championship’s 108th edition (with its 108 proof) and its return to Aronimink Golf Club in Newtown Square, Pennsylvania. (Hence, N and S.)

A bold chocolate character kicks things off on the nose, with layers of cinnamon giving the aromatics a Mexican chocolate quality. A light green herb character and more baking spices, particularly ginger, build from there, the more forceful abv finally showing its face, at least for a moment.

The chocolate is entirely dominant on the palate — I don’t know that I’ve tasted anything quite this expressive of cocoa in recent memory. It is, however, surprisingly tame on the tongue, the 54% abv not really making the impact telegraphed by the nose. Perhaps all that chocolate sauce has an appropriately tempering effect, the whiskey fading into wholly complementary notes of vanilla, more cinnamon, and crumbled graham crackers. The baking spice gets a bit hotter as the finish heats up, but things never spiral into anything unapproachable; this is a whiskey designed for sipping on the golf course, after all. Gentle touches of cedar wood and fresh tobacco — both wholly golf-appropriate, by the way — linger on a tidy but immersive finish. Like the 2024, this is a great value offering. 108 proof. A- / $38

summary:

The post Review: Wines of Ancient Peaks, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We cover the wines of Paso Robles’ Ancient Peaks with regularity, so these 2026 offerings should not come as a surprise. The value present in these bottlings, however, is more of a shock…

Updated late 2026 with the latest releases.

2024 Ancient Peaks Sauvignon Blanc Paso Robles – Quite tropical at first, this wine moves into grassier territory, with a slight astringency developing late in the game. Gentle white florals complement an emerging and insistent lemon peel character, giving the wine a clean, crisp finish. A- / $20

2024 Ancient Peaks Chardonnay Paso Robles Santa Margarita Ranch – Vanilla-laced but far from overwhelming, this is a refreshing and easygoing chardonnay with layers of vanilla, lychee, and honeysuckle — though all are quite balanced and restrained. Emerging lemon notes on the finish give the wine a custard-like quality, though it’s never overly sweet or overly woody. Pairs perfectly with lighter fare, though the rich body can hold up to spice and richness. Outstanding value. A- / $20

2023 Ancient Peaks Zinfandel Paso Robles Santa Margarita Ranch – This is a wine we’ve seen many times before, and this 2023 expression doesn’t change the formula dramatically — though it does build on its previous iterations. Notes of black cherries in syrup and chocolate sauce are expected and provide something of a holiday vibe — but it’s one which is quite sweet but also balanced by a gentle tartness. Those cherry notes and some light, herbal greenery inform a finish that feels a bit more elevated than previous renditions, although now at 15% abv, it’s certainly not because of any light-handedness in the vineyard. A- / $24

2022 Ancient Peaks Oyster Ridge Santa Margarita Ranch – This cab-heavy (65%) Bordeaux blend hits heavy with graphite and licorice from the start, meandering its way to notes of dense blackberry and prune, then cola and dark chocolate. Brooding but quite sweet, things build to a crescendo on the spice-dusted finish, which sees more dried fruits giving this wine an almost Port-like quality, laced with notes of chocolate-covered cherries. A bit too overripe this year, its 14.9% abv is hardly a surprise. B+ / $60

2022 Ancient Peaks Pearl Cabernet Sauvignon Santa Margarita Ranch – 100% cabernet in 100% new French oak makes for a decadent expression of the grape, and this 2022 Pearl hits all the high points for California cab, while keeping prices well below $100. While plenty boozy (another 14.9%er), the exuberant fruits, both black and red, currants and strawberries, crushed together with plums, leads the way to a lip-smacking midpalate that, eventually, finds its way to bittersweet chocolate and moderated baking spice to add a touch of nuance. While far less overtly sweet than Oyster Ridge, it’s equally decadent, almost chewy in its opulence, with lingering hints of cinnamon and nutmeg adding an exotic bent. Lovely. A / $72

title: Review: Wines of Dr. Konstantin Frank, 2026 Releases
summary:
More than any other American holiday, Thanksgiving demands quite a bit from the wine list. There needs to be something that can stand up to turkey, cut through whatever’s in the gravy and still work with that mystery dish your aunt brings that is of indeterminable origin. New York’s Konstantin Frank has inadvertently constructed a…

The post Review: Wines of Dr. Konstantin Frank, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
More than any other American holiday, Thanksgiving demands quite a bit from the wine list. There needs to be something that can stand up to turkey, cut through whatever’s in the gravy and still work with that mystery dish your aunt brings that is of indeterminable origin. New York’s Konstantin Frank has inadvertently constructed a lineup for this exact litmus test. Riesling remains one of the stable cores of their operations, bright enough to handle the richest of foods without flinching. However, the reds and rosé also earn their seat at the table, and today we’re checking out a trio suitable for the big dinner and every preference.

2025 Dr. Konstantin Frank Dry Riesling – While they may call this a dry Riesling, what pours in the glass clearly has other ideas. Lime zest, nectarine and cold apple leap out before even committing to a sip. There’s a slow, almost syrupy viscosity across the tongue, and a trace of sweetness cutting through from underneath. Acidity arrives at the right moment, bright and crisp as biting into an actual apple, and the orchard flavors stay put as the finish lingers. A steal at this price. A- / $20

2024 Dr. Konstantin Frank Old Vines Pinot Noir – Dried herbs, baking spices and a touch of graphite meld with red berries, giving this a lovely evocation of winter’s imminent arrival. As the palate progresses, the light body carries the fruit forward, but its balanced with a nice kick of clove. The finish carries on with a touch of chocolate and dark cherry, with tannins framing everything quite nicely. It’s incredibly approachable and versatile: it will pair well with a well-dressed turkey, but also as a solo standalone for when the relatives have left, the dishes are drying, and the silence of your house returns to provide merciful and sweet relief. A- / $28

2025 Dr. Konstantin Frank Cabernet Franc Rosé – There’s a surprisingly big and complex aroma of juicy cherry, fresh peach and a touch of floral influence on the nose, with a distinctive layer of mocha and oak cutting through with some time in the glass. The light-to-medium weight palate is rich with orange and fig, and there’s a slightly chalky edge to the finish, providing a bit of grit. It’s well-balanced and holds up incredibly well for the price point. This one deserves a spot on the table before the main event. B+ / $20
